entities.name: Gregorio di Montelongo
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gregorio di Montelongo (died September 15, 1269) was a formidable ecclesiastical and political figure of the High Middle Ages, serving first as Bishop of Tripoli (1249–1251) in the Latin East and subsequently as the powerful Patriarch of Aquileia (1251–1269). His career was defined by unwavering loyalty to the papacy during its protracted struggle with the Hohenstaufen emperors, particularly Frederick II and his son Conrad IV, and by his energetic, often militant, defense of the temporal and spiritual prerogatives of the Aquileian patriarchate in northeastern Italy. Montelongo's actions significantly shaped the political landscape of Friuli, Istria, and the Veneto, embedding the patriarchate deeply into the complex imperial-papal conflict that characterized mid-13th century Europe.

As Bishop of Tripoli, Montelongo was deeply involved in the precarious politics of the Crusader States, a period marked by constant external threats and internal divisions. His elevation to the Patriarchate of Aquileia in 1251 by Pope Innocent IV positioned him at the heart of imperial-papal contention. He served as a papal legate, actively campaigning against the Hohenstaufen, leading forces in the March of Ancona, and excommunicating imperial supporters. His military campaigns often brought him into conflict with regional powers, including Ezzelino III da Romano and the Count of Gorizia, as he sought to consolidate and expand the patriarchal domain against both secular and ecclesiastical rivals.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gregorio di Montelongo was a pivotal figure in the 13th-century struggle between the Papacy and the Hohenstaufen, playing a direct military and political role that contributed to the imperial dynasty's downfall. His tenure profoundly shaped the political and territorial development of the Patriarchate of Aquileia, cementing its regional power for decades.
